column3: A tall tower on the Gan River in Nanchang, one of the Three Great Towers of southern China, made famous by a Tang poem that every schoolchild learns.
A museum in the former building where, on August 1, 1927, an armed uprising took place in Nanchang, marking the founding of the Red Army.
An old pagoda in the middle of Nanchang, built to protect the city from fire. It stands among streets of snack stalls.
A museum for the painter Bada Shanren, or Zhu Da, a Ming prince who became a monk and painted lonely birds and fish.
A Taoist temple tied to the worship of Xu Xun, a local hero said to have tamed floods. Jiangxi people took the cult across China.
Rice noodles tossed with chili, soy sauce and pickles, and served with a bowl of clear soup. A breakfast classic in Nanchang.
Soup simmered for hours in clay jars over charcoal, with chicken, ribs or other ingredients, a Nanchang comfort food.
A stir-fry of crisp wormwood stems from the lake shore with smoked pork, a seasonal Jiangxi favorite.
Tiny, transparent fish from Poyang Lake, cooked with egg or in soup, light and tender.
Rice noodles stir-fried with egg, vegetables and chili, a quick and filling Nanchang favorite.
A folk theater that grew from the songs of tea pickers, with lively humor and acting, popular in Jiangxi's villages.
A masked ritual dance performed to drive away evil spirits, with colorful wooden masks, and a very old tradition in Jiangxi.
The site of the imperial kilns where porcelain was made for the Ming and Qing courts, with ruins and a museum.
A park of old kilns and workshops where visitors can watch potters throw, paint and fire porcelain by hand.
A former porcelain factory area converted into studios, galleries, cafés and a market for young artists.
A museum that follows Chinese ceramics from early pottery through to the high point of Jingdezhen porcelain.
Jingdezhen has made fine white porcelain for over a thousand years, known as the porcelain capital of the world.
Cold rice noodles with a spicy sauce, a refreshing local snack in the hot summer.
A pan-fried fish cake made from minced fish, with a springy bite, served as a snack or in soup.
Blue and white porcelain is painted by hand with cobalt blue under the glaze. Jingdezhen's pieces were prized from Persia to Europe.
Fencai is a porcelain style that uses soft, painted enamels, with delicate pinks and greens, and was loved at the Qing court.
A misty mountain of waterfalls, peaks and old villas, a retreat for poets, scholars and officials for centuries. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A tall waterfall that the Tang poet Li Bai compared to the Milky Way falling from heaven.
One of the four great academies of ancient China, at the foot of Mount Lu, where Zhu Xi taught in the 12th century.
China's largest freshwater lake, which shrinks and grows with the seasons. In winter, many cranes and other migratory birds gather here.
A temple at the foot of Mount Lu, regarded as the birthplace of the Pure Land school of Buddhism.
A kind of mountain frog found in the streams of Lushan, cooked in a savory dish, a local delicacy.
Crabs from Poyang Lake are in season in the autumn, steamed and eaten with ginger and vinegar.
The poet Tao Yuanming gave up an official post to live in the countryside in Jiangxi, and his poems on fields and chrysanthemums are still loved.
A wall dating from the Song dynasty, surrounding old Ganzhou, among the oldest city walls in China that is still standing.
A group of red sandstone cliffs and caves with Buddhist statues carved in the Tang and Song dynasties.
Sweet navel oranges from southern Jiangxi, famed across China, and harvested in winter.
A fiery stir-fry of freshwater fish with chili, garlic and herbs, a staple of southern Jiangxi.
Tofu stuffed with minced pork and simmered, a Hakka comfort dish in southern Jiangxi.
A mountain of strange granite pillars and peaks that look like people and animals, wrapped in mist. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A county of villages with white walls and black roofs, among tea fields and fields of golden rapeseed flowers in spring, called the most beautiful countryside in China.
The home of the Celestial Masters of Taoism, a landscape of red cliffs and a clear river, with cliff tombs.
Sweet pastries and rice cakes made in Wuyuan's villages, a snack for tourists and a gift.
A chewy rice cake made in Yiyang, eaten with sauce or fried, a New Year tradition.
A fragrant green tea from the misty hills of Wuyuan, with a fresh and lasting taste.
Rice grown in selenium-rich soil near Yichun, marketed as a healthy and flavorful rice.
A tea grown in the selenium-rich soil of Yichun, with a gentle flavor.
A forested mountain range where Mao Zedong and Zhu De set up the first rural base of the Chinese Communist revolution in 1927.
An old academy on an island in the Gan River, founded in the Song dynasty, which produced many officials.
A mountain in Ji'an with an old temple, where a major school of Chan Buddhism developed.
A simple meal of red rice and pumpkin soup that recalls the plain food of the Red Army in the 1920s.
Jianchang is a school of traditional herbal medicine, known for its way of preparing herbs.
A tiny, sweet mandarin grown in Nanfeng for over a thousand years and once sent as a tribute to the emperor.
The home of the Taoist Celestial Masters for about 60 generations, in Yingtan, the center of the Zhengyi school.
A tea grown on the slopes of Dragon-Tiger Mountain, with a fresh, floral aroma.
A mountain with a high alpine meadow, where visitors camp to watch the sun rise above a sea of clouds.
Pingxiang's fried rice noodles are chewy and spicy, stir-fried with pork, and are the signature dish of the town.
Sweet, juicy tangerines that Xinyu has grown for a long time, picked in late autumn.
